entry.name: M4
entry.description: Catalog class M4 is the habitable primary: a star about one solar radius across, shining at roughly one solar luminosity, photosphere a warm gold that can slide toward pale yellow or soft orange at the limb. It is not a red dwarf. The light that fills a cockpit after JUMP is the color of late afternoon on a living world — thick enough to warm a faceplate, gentle enough that open air and green can exist near one AU. Ultraviolet is present but not cruel. You have arrived under a lamp that already knows how to keep cities and farms without canned breath.

entry.name: K2
entry.description: A K2 orange dwarf sits smaller than the Sun, perhaps four-fifths of a solar radius, and pours out only about two-fifths of a solar luminosity. The disk is deep amber, almost the color of cooling iron, brighter at the center and rust-dark at the edge. It will outlive any yellow analog by billions of years. Inner dust is a kiln: dry, oxide-stained, too close for open water. Past the ice line the same long, quiet heat lets freeze-concentrated brines work alkali salts out of silicate rock. You did not come for the baked plains. You came for the cold chemistry that only this patient orange lamp allows.

entry.name: M1
entry.description: An M1 red dwarf is a coal of a star: roughly half a solar radius, a few percent of a solar luminosity, the photosphere a deep wine-red that never quite becomes white even at noon. Any distance that could melt ice hugs the primary so tightly the sky is a swollen ember. The belt rides that glare. Flares rise without warning — a sudden white stitch across the red — and the rocks have never fully degassed. Nickel-iron and rare-earth oxides still sit in the metal phase, waiting. Arrival feels like docking beside a furnace that has been burning since before your species learned names.

entry.name: K5
entry.description: A K5 orange dwarf is cooler and dimmer than K2: about seven-tenths of a solar radius, perhaps a sixth of a solar luminosity, the color of copper left in a forge. The light is smoky orange, never gold, never the clean yellow of a habitable-class lamp. Inner dust and vulcan moons live in that heat. Carbon has been cooked past peat into hard, nuclear-grade lattice. Fumaroles sweat borate salts. There is no biosphere to soften the view. When the Gate drops you here the star looks close enough to touch and far too old to care that you have come.

entry.name: M0
entry.description: This M0 is not a tidy dwarf. It is giant-class: tens of solar radii across, swollen, a dull blood-red disk that can fill a viewport the way a planet should not. Luminosity is huge — hundreds of suns — but the light is lazy and cold at the edge, all long wavelengths. The ice line has been pushed far into the dark. Outer ices keep nebular noble gases adsorbed on grain surfaces like breath on glass. Warm dust will disappoint you. The prize is out where the red has faded to black and the star still looks too large to be that distant.

entry.name: G8
entry.description: A G8 young solar analog is almost familiar: near nine-tenths of a solar radius, perhaps four-fifths of a solar luminosity, photosphere a butter-yellow that should feel like home. It does not. The disk is still restless. Ultraviolet from a young chromosphere is high enough to sting instruments and drive nitrogen-oxygen chemistry in dry pans. Evaporite oxidizer salts bleach the dust. Carbonaceous belts still hold ice and organics, but this is not a garden. The yellow looks like welcome and reads, on a spectrometer, like a warning.

entry.name: K3
entry.description: A K3 orange dwarf stands between K2 and K5: about three-quarters of a solar radius, roughly a fifth of a solar luminosity, the color of a pumpkin lantern or a banked fire. The inner world is a light-metal residue — residual melts and impactites, structural alkali-earths and ballast copper-family metals, no air, no farms. The star is neither kind nor spectacular. It simply burns, orange and even, over a crust that was never invited to live. Arrival is quiet. The loneliness is the point.

entry.name: ssassm
entry.description: Construction of spacecraft hulls is a marvel of advanced engineering and precision. Floating serenely in the vacuum of space, is a hub of activity, with robotic arms and drones tirelessly working to assemble the skeletal frameworks of future starships. The process begins with the creation of the hull, a robust and versatile structure designed to withstand the rigors of space travel. Advanced materials, lightweight yet incredibly strong, are meticulously welded and fused together by automated systems. These materials are chosen for their durability, resistance to cosmic radiation, and ability to endure extreme temperature fluctuations. The hulls are constructed in modular sections, each piece fitting together with the precision of a jigsaw puzzle. This modular approach allows for flexibility in design, enabling the shipyard to produce a variety of hull configurations tailored to different mission profiles. Whether it's a sleek exploration vessel, a formidable warship, or a massive cargo freighter, the basic hull can be adapted to meet the specific needs of the mission. Once the hull is complete, it is moved to the next stage of assembly, where it will be outfitted with various modules. These modules, pre-fabricated and tested, are designed for a range of uses: living quarters [crwqrt], command bridges [cbridg], cargo bays [cargob], and more. Each module is equipped with standardized interfaces, allowing them to be easily connected and integrated into the hull. Robotic arms and drones carefully maneuver the modules into place, securing them with precision and ensuring all connections are airtight and functional. The interior of the ship begins to take shape, with corridors, rooms, and systems coming together to form a cohesive whole. Advanced AI oversees the entire process, monitoring for any anomalies and ensuring that every component meets stringent quality standards. This assembly technology represents the pinnacle of human ingenuity and collaboration, a testament to our ability to create complex, adaptable, and resilient spacecraft. Each hull, filled with its specialized modules, is a blank canvas, ready to be transformed into a vessel capable of exploring the farthest reaches of the cosmos.

entry.name: filidx
entry.description: Imagine a cutting-edge digital library, where advanced file indexing technology forms the backbone of a vast repository of knowledge. This system, designed to support researchers, operates with the precision and efficiency, ensuring that every piece of information is easily accessible and meticulously organized. The process begins with the ingestion of data from a multitude of sources: academic journals, books, research papers and multimedia files. These content of the digital files analyzed by sophisticated algorithms that can recognize text, images, videos and both complex data structures and unorganized raw data. Each file is then tagged creating a rich, searchable index. At the heart of this technology is a powerful indexing engine, capable of processing vast amounts of data in real-time. This engine uses advanced techniques such as natural language processing and machine learning to understand the context and relevance of each document. It can identify relationships between different pieces of information, linking related documents and creating a web of interconnected knowledge. Researchers can query the library. The system can handle natural language questions, returning results that are not only relevant but also ranked by their significance and reliability.
